title: Can GPT-3 mark writing? The data is in...
author: Daisy Christodoulou and Chris Wheadon
source: Daisy Christodoulou and Chris Wheadon (substack.nomoremarking.com), March 21, 2023
summary: No More Marking reports a trial of GPT-3 marking against teacher Comparative Judgement across eight schools, using Year 5 and Year 7 typed essays on an ideal job. The AI's marks correlated with human scores at only 0.66 and 0.69, and the AI clustered its grades between 2 and 5, which inflates the apparent agreement. Outliers showed judgements the authors could not explain, and attempts to improve the prompts or mark schemes mostly made things worse. The authors conclude that GPT-style models are not yet good enough for school or large-scale assessment, and they pre-empt two common rebuttals: that humans are imperfect too, and that the AI will simply improve. Their move is to answer enthusiasm with systematic data rather than one-off examples.
points: A trial with 40 scripts found human-AI correlations of just 0.66 (Year 5) and 0.69 (Year 7), well below what reliable marking requires.
AI marks clustered in a narrow band, so the headline correlation overstates real agreement and the model fails to separate weak scripts.
The fair test for AI marking is whether it beats human judgement, and here it did not beat traditional marking or Comparative Judgement.
The types of errors matter as much as their rate, and the authors argue the AI's errors would harm teaching and learning more than human ones.
Faith that the AI will get better is unwarranted, since there is no guarantee any technology keeps improving.
quotes: The internal reliability of both the Comparative Judgement tasks was 0.85.
First, the AI clustered its results between grades 2 & 5. Very few scripts were awarded 1, 6, 7 or 8. This clustering inflates the human-AI correlation, making it seem better than it is.
In both year 5 and year 7, the AI awarded its lowest grade of 2 to scripts ranging from 0 – 50 on the human scale. It’s failing to differentiate between these scripts.
We tried a number of different methods and mark schemes to improve the AI judging accuracy. Most of them made it worse! The results here are its best performance.
Based on these results, we do not think that AI assessment using large language models like GPT is good enough to be used in schools or in large-scale assessments at the moment.
Not only that, but the types of mistakes matter, and the types of mistakes the AI makes are likely to have more of a negative impact on teaching and learning than those made by humans.
There is no guarantee that any technology will keep improving, and our experience so far has made us more sceptical.
